Frozen controlled routing v2 — all 15 development cases

16 October 2026 · GPT-5.4-mini · medium · 8000 completion-token ceiling · 15 fresh calls.

11/15 stored next-action matches (73.3%). All 15 responses finish normally and pass the structured assessment/controller contract. The saved original full run had 9/15 matches.

This is next-action label agreement, not verified answer accuracy. Clarification remains 3/6, and some correctly routed answers are incomplete. An identical-request repeat loses a previously included workflow-stage edit. The candidate remains experimental.

Fixed candidate and test scope

The user authorized one full development run after limited diagnostics. The exact controlled-routing-v2 prompt, schema, routing code and answer assembler were frozen before this run. Every case received one fresh model call, including the three previously sampled cases; no prior result was substituted. There was no tuning during the run, automatic repair, retry, paid grader or tracker write.

Inputs are the manually annotated corpus-passage development set: 40 source-record appearances, 22 distinct records and 81 selected passages. Source/passages counts vary by case and are not the older six-chunk retrieval setup. A source record is the original document, issue or comment; a passage is a selected excerpt from it. No retrieval, embedding or held-out test material was used. Labels were read only after provider calls and remain unchanged.

Content review, separate from routing

Assistant inspection categories: 2 usable by inspection, 8 needing minor revision and 5 needing material revision. These are source-based review judgments, not independent accuracy percentages. No application was run or independently human-approved. Some action-label mismatches are defensible support alternatives; a label match can still contain a material technical error.

Controller guarantees and limits

The model supplies a typed assessment, not a final action. The controller prioritizes concrete required human review, then useful material user-providable gaps, then a supported answer with no material gap, then ordinary internal investigation. It also enforces trusted question/refinement limits and preserves generated answer edits. It cannot detect a semantic gap omitted by the model, prove source applicability, or add a missing code correction.

All 16 identified corrections on answer routes appear in the actual replies. All 85 copied report blocks and their hashes match the supplied original text. Environment metadata is copied exactly for every case; the three empty input environments are DEV-9342, DEV-4325 and DEV-5591. Provenance verifies origin, not correct interpretation or complete selection.

Identical-request repeats

The three earlier sampled cases were called again with byte-equivalent requests. Their action labels remain unchanged, but content varies. In DEV-4325 the prior sample included a persistent-stage correction that the fresh sample omitted. Therefore the earlier single-output success did not establish stable workflow coverage.

DEV-5604 — text_area inside an expander doesn't load from session state

Expected request_info · actual escalate · needs_revision

Skips the initialization discriminator and escalates with unsupported hydration certainty.

Useful part: Recognizes the fragile whole-state guard in a raw finding and preserves the reported expander/button symptom.

  • The assessment records no information gap even though a key-specific initialization comparison remains useful. A raw finding notices the broad guard but that does not influence routing.
  • The final reply treats initialization as settled and rules out direct app-code issues too strongly. Source guidance and historical analogies do not establish the reported 1.13.0 cause.
  • A finding says the symptom must come from hydration rather than a later mutation; absence of a later assignment does not prove that mechanism.

Actual fresh user reply

Maintainer review is needed: A keyed text area inside an expander does not hydrate from existing session state after the app reruns from the button/spinner path and the expander is opened later. The shown code initializes state before widget creation and does not overwrite `text` later, while official docs say keyed widgets are associated with session state and existing widgets should reconnect on rerun. The symptom therefore looks like an expander/widget-state interaction issue rather than a direct application-code error, and the current sources do not establish a verified fix for Streamlit 1.13.0. [R5][R7][R12][R16][S1][S2][S3][S4]
Saved original policy-v3 reply for comparison
The supplied code already initializes Session State before rendering the keyed `text_area`, so the empty field after the button/expander sequence is not explained by missing app initialization [S1][S2]. The widget is only rendered inside the expander, and the documented widget lifecycle says reruns reconnect existing widgets when their command is called again; the reported behavior therefore looks like a synchronization problem on the closed-expander path rather than a local code-order bug [S3][S4]. A historical report shows the same expander/state-retention pattern in another keyed widget, which supports a product-level investigation for Streamlit 1.13.0 [S5][S6].

        "start_line": 7,
        "end_line": 19,
        "text": "### Initialize values in Session State\n\nThe Session State API follows a field-based API, which is very similar to Python dictionaries:\n\n```python\n# Initialization\nif 'key' not in st.session_state:\n    st.session_state['key'] = 'value'\n\n# Session State also supports attribute based syntax\nif 'key' not in st.session_state:\n    st.session_state.key = 'value'\n```",
        "text_sha256": "32e6c93872df2a0db478652b12c8821a06805a5777e4c93909018bde593f57b4"
      },
      {
        "span_id": "DEV-5604-S01-P02",
        "start_char": 1751,
        "end_char": 1959,
        "start_line": 71,
        "end_line": 80,
        "text": "### Session State and Widget State association\n\nEvery widget with a key is automatically added to Session State:\n\n```python\nst.text_input(\"Your name\", key=\"name\")\n\n# This exists now:\nst.session_state.name\n```",
        "text_sha256": "8577cfb2ae94a2729060d0873b55a6eafd7ea09835956e0f4c2e1973242c791a"
      }
    ]
  },

        "start_line": 209,
        "end_line": 213,
        "text": "## Widget life cycle\n\nWhen a widget command is called, Streamlit will check if it already has a widget with the same identity. Streamlit will reconnect if it thinks the widget already exists. Otherwise, it will make a new one.\n\nAs mentioned earlier, Streamlit determines a widget's identity differently based on if it has a key. The page name also factors into a widget's identity, where widget identites are not preserved between pages. On the other hand, callback functions, callback args and kwargs, label visibility, and disabling a widget never affect a widget's identity.",
        "text_sha256": "d43782c4d80abbacfe4458d901434116482fdfa18c2fe1327526c15d129bcd5a"
      },
      {
        "span_id": "DEV-5604-S02-P02",
        "start_char": 16050,
        "end_char": 16547,
        "start_line": 229,
        "end_line": 235,
        "text": "### Calling a widget command when the widget already exists\n\nWhen rerunning a script without changing a widget's identity:\n\n1. Streamlit will connect to the existing frontend and backend parts.\n2. If the widget has a key that was deleted from `st.session_state`, then Streamlit will recreate the key using the current frontend value. This is because deleting a key from Session State will not revert the widget to a default value.\n3. The widget command will return the current value of the widget.",
        "text_sha256": "a38190baf3ad45952b5809c6bccbb9daecfe81e684b5d65183868d8dd82bc90a"
      }

S1

### Initialize values in Session State

The Session State API follows a field-based API, which is very similar to Python dictionaries:

```python
# Initialization
if 'key' not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state['key'] = 'value'

# Session State also supports attribute based syntax
if 'key' not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.key = 'value'
```

S2

### Session State and Widget State association

Every widget with a key is automatically added to Session State:

```python
st.text_input("Your name", key="name")

# This exists now:
st.session_state.name
```

S3

## Widget life cycle

When a widget command is called, Streamlit will check if it already has a widget with the same identity. Streamlit will reconnect if it thinks the widget already exists. Otherwise, it will make a new one.

As mentioned earlier, Streamlit determines a widget's identity differently based on if it has a key. The page name also factors into a widget's identity, where widget identites are not preserved between pages. On the other hand, callback functions, callback args and kwargs, label visibility, and disabling a widget never affect a widget's identity.

S4

### Calling a widget command when the widget already exists

When rerunning a script without changing a widget's identity:

1. Streamlit will connect to the existing frontend and backend parts.
2. If the widget has a key that was deleted from `st.session_state`, then Streamlit will recreate the key using the current frontend value. This is because deleting a key from Session State will not revert the widget to a default value.
3. The widget command will return the current value of the widget.

```
import streamlit as st

with st.expander("expander:"):
    value=st.number_input("number",value=1.,key="vl_key"); # insert a values

st.write(st.session_state["vl_key"])

def update_value():
    st.session_state["vl_key"] = 0.;

update_button=st.button('Update',on_click=update_value)

st.write(st.session_state["vl_key"])

print_value=st.button('Print value')
if print_value:
    st.write(st.session_state["vl_key"])

```

1. Open the expander and input a value, for example 10. Click enter and close the expander.
2. Click the update value button. The value is updated to 0.
3. Click the print button. The value returns to 10.
4. Note that if the same procedure is repeated BUT the expander is left open, then the value stays equal to 0. 

**Expected behavior:**

I expect the value to be equal to 0, regardless if the expander is left open or closed

**Actual behavior:**

The value changes back to 10 when the expander is closed

Expected request_info · actual request_info · minor_revision

Useful focused question about an unshown same-key assignment; no cause is asserted as observed.

Useful part: Keeps a material user-providable gap alongside possible internal investigation, allowing the controller to ask before escalating.

  • A same-key write is a supported hypothesis, not a confirmed cause. A duplicate widget key is not independently established to cause this exact exception.
  • The negative hypothetical reply moves directly to escalation without establishing that all other useful checks are exhausted.
  • A raw finding says to keep a key only for reading state. Keys also serve widget identity; that optional workaround statement is too narrow and is correctly absent from the actual question reply.

Actual fresh user reply

The docs say a data editor key is stored in Session State and that its state cannot be programmatically set; a same-key write would explain the exception, while absence of any such write would leave a version-specific framework issue unresolved. [S2][S3][S4][R6][R16]

Is `st.session_state['companies_df']` assigned or mutated anywhere else in the app, or is `companies_df` used as a key for any other widget?
Saved original policy-v3 reply for comparison
One missing detail will determine whether this is a key-collision issue or a framework-level behavior: I need to know whether your app assigns or initializes `st.session_state['companies_df']` anywhere else, or reuses `companies_df` as another widget key. That check would show whether the exception is coming from setting the data editor’s read-only Session State value [S2][S3].

Do you assign, initialize, or otherwise write to `st.session_state['companies_df']` anywhere else in the app (or reuse `companies_df` as another widget key)?

S2

key
          (str, int, or None)

 

An optional string or integer to use as the unique key for
the widget. If this is None (default), a key will be
generated for the widget based on the values of the other
parameters. No two widgets may have the same key.

A key lets you access the widget's value via
st.session_state[key] (read-only). For more details, see
[Widget behavior](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/concepts/architecture/widget-behavior).

S3

The state is stored in a read-only dictionary-like object that
supports both key and attribute notation. Top-level assignment and
nested dict mutation raise TypeError. List fields (added_rows,
deleted_rows) are ordinary lists and are not frozen. Data editor
states cannot be programmatically changed or set through Session State.

S4

Dataframes
Evidence role: Official documentation excerpt; match the source snapshot to the user version.

### Access edited data

Sometimes, it is more convenient to know which cells have been changed rather than getting the entire edited dataframe back. Streamlit makes this easy through the use of [Session State](/develop/concepts/architecture/session-state). If a `key` parameter is set, Streamlit will store any changes made to the dataframe in Session State.

This snippet shows how you can access changed data using Session State:

Python

```python
st.data_editor(df, key="my_key", num_rows="dynamic") # 👈 Set a key
st.write("Here's the value in Session State:")
st.write(st.session_state["my_key"]) # 👈 Show the value in Session State
```

In this code snippet, the `key` parameter is set to `"my_key"`. After the data editor is created, the value associated to `"my_key"` in Session State is displayed in the app using `st.write`. This shows the additions, edits, and deletions that were made.

The cited widget docs are versioned/snapshot-based, and the report did not include a version; knowing the release determines whether this is current behavior, a regression, or already fixed. [R18][S2][S3][S6]

Which Streamlit version are you running?
Saved original policy-v3 reply for comparison
The repro shows an event-driven Session State write putting `st.number_input` into an out-of-range value and then trapping the widget in a bad editing state [R8][R10][R20]. The docs confirm that widget keys map to `st.session_state[key]` and that callbacks run before the app reruns [S2][S5], but they also describe direct post-instantiation Session State mutation as disallowed [S6]. That leaves the reported case in the allowed callback/update path, so the missing range validation appears to be a framework behavior issue rather than something an app-side workaround can fully resolve [R4][S1][S3].

R3

I believe this applies to `st.slider` as well, but for `st.number_input`:

R4

If you declare the widget with a default value that violates `min_value` or `max_value`, an error is raised. However, if you assign such a value through Session State, the widget takes on the incorrect value without (Python) warning.

R8

```Python

import streamlit as st



value = st.number_input("A",min_value=1, max_value=5, key="A")



def set_too_big():

    st.session_state.A = 10



st.button("Too big", on_click=set_too_big)



st.write(value)

```

1. Run the app

2. Click the button to programattically set a value greater than the declared max

3. Observe the widget returns the too-large value

4. Click the minus on the widget and get stuck in an editing state for the widget until the bad value is resolved

- Streamlit version:

S1

min_value
          (int, float, or None)

        The minimum permitted value.
If this is None (default), there will be no minimum for float
values and a minimum of - (1<<53) + 1 for integer values.

          max_value
          (int, float, or None)

        The maximum permitted value.
If this is None (default), there will be no maximum for float
values and a maximum of (1<<53) - 1 for integer values.

          value
          (int, float, "min" or None)

        The value of this widget when it first renders. If this is
"min" (default), the initial value is min_value unless
min_value is None. If min_value is None, the widget
initializes with a value of 0.0 or 0.
If value is None, the widget will initialize with no value
and return None until the user provides input.

S2

key
          (str, int, or None)

        An optional string or integer to use as the unique key for
the widget. If this is None (default), a key will be
generated for the widget based on the values of the other
parameters. No two widgets may have the same key. Assigning
a key stabilizes the widget's identity and preserves its
state across reruns even when other parameters change.
A key lets you read or update the widget's value via
st.session_state[key]. For more details, see Widget
behavior.

S3

min_value
          (a supported type or None)

 

The minimum permitted value.
If this is None (default), the minimum value depends on the
type as follows:

- integer: 0

- float: 0.0

- date or datetime: value - timedelta(days=14)

- time: time.min

max_value
          (a supported type or None)

 

The maximum permitted value.
If this is None (default), the maximum value depends on the
type as follows:

- integer: 100

- float: 1.0

- date or datetime: value + timedelta(days=14)

- time: time.max

value
          (a supported type or a tuple/list of supported types or None)

 

The value of the slider when it first renders. If a tuple/list
of two values is passed here, then a range slider with those lower
and upper bounds is rendered. For example, if set to (1, 10) the
slider will have a selectable range between 1 and 10.
This defaults to min_value. If the type is not otherwise
specified in any of the numeric parameters, the widget will have an
integer value.

S4

A key lets you read or update the widget's value via
st.session_state[key]. For more details, see [Widget
behavior](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/concepts/architecture/widget-behavior).

S5

### Use Callbacks to update Session State

A callback is a python function which gets called when an input widget changes.

**Order of execution**: When updating Session state in response to **events**, a callback function gets executed first, and then the app is executed from top to bottom.

Callbacks can be used with widgets using the parameters `on_change` (or `on_click`), `args`, and `kwargs`:

**Parameters**

- **on_change** or **on_click** - The function name to be used as a callback
- **args** (_tuple_) - List of arguments to be passed to the callback function
- **kwargs** (_dict_) - Named arguments to be passed to the callback function

S6

- Modifying the value of a widget via the Session state API, after instantiating it, is not allowed and will raise a `StreamlitAPIException`. For example:

  ```python
  slider = st.slider(
      label='My Slider', min_value=1,
      max_value=10, value=5, key='my_slider')

  st.session_state.my_slider = 7

  # Throws an exception!
  ```

DEV-4338 — Inconsistent session state behavior when used with widgets

Expected answer · actual escalate · minor_revision

Escalation differs from the stored answer label but preserves the unresolved historical first-value symptom.

Useful part: Does not claim modern cleanup guidance proves a fix for both reported symptoms; retains the affected old version range and separates first-render seeding from cleanup.

  • The stored answerable category also contains a second historical symptom not fully resolved by the supplied sources. Count the action mismatch while flagging this scope ambiguity for team adjudication; do not relabel it.

Actual fresh user reply

Maintainer review is needed: In Streamlit 0.89.0–1.5.0, a session_state value initialized before a keyed widget is first rendered is reported not to seed that widget, and the value is later reset/cleared when the widget is hidden and re-shown. The shown code does not contain an obvious app-side assignment mistake, while the documentation only establishes widget cleanup on non-render and later keyed-widget semantics changes; it does not fully explain the reported first-render seeding failure in the affected version range. Maintainer/product review is needed to determine whether this is a historical regression or an expected limitation for those versions. [R5][R7][R10][R12][R14][S2][S3][S5]
Saved original policy-v3 reply for comparison
The first symptom is explained by documented widget cleanup when a widget is no longer rendered, but the second symptom still conflicts with the same-key hydration flow described in the docs and release note context for 0.89.0. Because the report spans older versions and the supplied material does not fully resolve whether the second behavior is an intended historical change or a regression, this needs maintainer review rather than an app-side workaround alone.

        "end_line": 26,
        "text": "**Key-based widget identity (v1.55.0)**\n\nAs of v1.55.0, all widgets support key-based identity. When a `key` is provided, the key is the primary determinant of the widget's identity, and changing other parameters (like `label`, `options`, or `default`) won't reset the widget. Some parameters that constrain valid values still affect identity for specific widgets, even when a key is provided. For example, changing `min_value` or `max_value` for `st.slider` will reset the widget because the current value could be invalidated. These exceptions are noted in each widget's `key` parameter description.\n\nKey-based identity was progressively introduced from v1.50.0 through v1.55.0. R2

Session state in Streamlit 0.89.0 to 1.5.0 has a strange behavior when bound to widgets (`key` parameter).

R5

1. In the same script run, initialize a session state item, and display a widget bound to it.

2. Make the widget disappear (by unchecking a checkbox for instance).

3. Reload with `R`. **ISSUE: Session state item doesn't exist anymore.**

4. Reload again multiple times. **ISSUE: Session state is cleared every other run.**

R7

1. In a first script run, initialize a session state item.

2. In a second run, display a widget bound to the previous session state item (by checking a checkbox for instance).  

    **ISSUE: Widget does not take value from session state.**

3. Change widget value, it updates the session state item correctly.

4. Make the widget disappear.

5. Reload with `R`. **ISSUE: Session state item resets to its initial value**.

```python
st.set_page_config(layout="wide")



c1, c2 = st.columns(2)



with c1:
```

R14

- Streamlit version: 0.89.0 to 1.5.0

- Python version: 3.8.6 (pyenv)

S1

**Key-based widget identity (v1.55.0)**

As of v1.55.0, all widgets support key-based identity. When a `key` is provided, the key is the primary determinant of the widget's identity, and changing other parameters (like `label`, `options`, or `default`) won't reset the widget. Some parameters that constrain valid values still affect identity for specific widgets, even when a key is provided. For example, changing `min_value` or `max_value` for `st.slider` will reset the widget because the current value could be invalidated. These exceptions are noted in each widget's `key` parameter description.

Key-based identity was progressively introduced from v1.50.0 through v1.55.0. If you're using an older version, check the [release notes](/develop/quick-reference/release-notes) to see which widgets support key-based identity in your version.

S2

### Widgets do not persist when not continually rendered

If a widget command for a specific widget instance isn't called during a script run, then none of its parts are retained, including its value in `st.session_state`. If a widget has a key and you navigate away from that widget, its key and associated value in `st.session_state` are deleted. Even temporarily hiding a widget causes it to reset when it reappears; Streamlit will treat it like a new widget. To preserve widget state across pages or when widgets are temporarily hidden, save the value to a separate placeholder key as shown below.

S3

### Calling a widget command when the widget doesn't already exist

If your script rerun calls a widget command with a changed identity or calls a widget command that wasn't used on the last script run:

1. Streamlit will build the frontend and backend parts of the widget, using its default value.
2. If the widget has been assigned a key, Streamlit will check if that key already exists in Session State.
   a. If the key exists and **isn't** associated to a widget with a different identity, Streamlit will assign that key's value to the widget.
   b. If the key exists and is associated to a widget with a different identity, Streamlit will overwrite the key-value pair with the default value. This is why writing to Session State before the widget command is important when [retaining statefulness across identity changes](#retain-statefulness-when-changing-a-widgets-identity).
   c. If the key doesn't exist, Streamlit will create a new key-value pair with the default value.
3. If there are args or kwargs for a callback function, they are evaluated and saved in memory.
4. The widget value is then returned by the function.

For step 2, prior to v1.46.0, Streamlit would ignore the value in Session State if it came from an instance of the widget on another page. This is because a widget on another page necessarily has a different identity. As of v1.46.0, Streamlit deletes such values at the beginning of a script run on a new page.

S4

### Widget clean-up process

Streamlit cleans up widget data at the end of every script run and at the beginning of a script run on a new page.

When Streamlit gets to the end of a script run, it will delete the data for any widgets it has in memory that were not rendered on the screen. Most importantly, that means Streamlit will delete all key-value pairs in `st.session_state` associated with a widget not currently on screen. When you switch pages, Streamlit will delete all data associated with widgets from the previous page.

S5

Issue context: unexpected session_state behavior with keys
Evidence role: Historical diagnostic discussion or proposed workaround; not a verified fix.

We took a bit of time to think about this, and in version 0.89.0 (due to be released soon, most likely tomorrow), the semantics of keyed widgets will change so that session state keys corresponding to widgets will only be present in the `st.session_state` dictionary if the widget exists as well. Because of this, you'll need to explicitly set `st.session_state` keys to have the values persist to achieve the behavior you're looking for.

This is a bit of a change from the current behavior (which didn't quite work as expected due to the bug described in this issue), but we decided to have things behave this way so that the semantics between keyed and unkeyed widgets are identical (that is, widget values are not persisted in either case if the widget is not present in the app).

S6

Streamlit 0.89.0 (2021-09-22)
Changes

- We've modified session state to reset widgets if any of their arguments changed even if they provide a key.
  - Some widget behavior may have changed, but we believe this change makes the most sense. We have added a section to [our documentation](/develop/concepts/widget-semantics) describing how they behave.

DEV-6166 — Session State remains after the tab is closed

Expected escalate · actual escalate · needs_revision

Appropriate escalation direction, but loop-exit reasoning still confuses script interruption and normal completion.

Useful part: Now cites the many-tab observation and distinguishes the shown shutdown path from the unknown timing before that path starts.

  • The loop never removes its condition key; key existence is not browser connection status. The response does not explicitly explain that distinction.
  • A stop request or script interruption does not imply normal exit from the while loop or execution of the following print. The findings still tie the post-loop print too directly to shutdown detection.
  • Batch cleanup can motivate investigation but does not verify asynchronous scheduling. Later community observations are not a verified fix for 1.18.1.
  • R20 is cited in the final reply but omitted from the six copied observations and the short summary. Preserve this useful clue explicitly in a practical handoff.

Actual fresh user reply

Maintainer review is needed: Session teardown after browser-tab close is delayed in the reported environment, so the example loop keeps running before the exit message prints. The supplied docs say session state is lost when the tab closes, but the report on Streamlit 1.18.1 says cleanup can lag significantly; the sources show the shutdown path once teardown starts, not what governs the delay before it starts. [R3][R11][R14][R20][S2][S3]
Saved original policy-v3 reply for comparison
The supplied report and references point to a timing discrepancy between tab close and session teardown, but the available evidence does not establish an immediate-disconnect guarantee or a version-specific regression. The code path shown requests script stop and then proceeds through shutdown cleanup [S3], while the docs only state that Session State is lost when the tab is closed [S2]. Because the main question is about cleanup/synchronization timing in Streamlit 1.18.1 rather than an app-side workaround, this needs maintainer review against the reported version and shutdown path behavior.

S1

## What is State?

We define access to a Streamlit app in a browser tab as a **session**. For each browser tab that connects to the Streamlit server, a new session is created. Streamlit reruns your script from top to bottom every time you interact with your app. Each reruns takes place in a blank slate: no variables are shared between runs.

Session State is a way to share variables between reruns, for each user session. In addition to the ability to store and persist state, Streamlit also exposes the ability to manipulate state using Callbacks. Session state also persists across pages inside a [multipage app](/develop/concepts/multipage-apps).

S2

### Caveats and limitations

Here are some limitations to keep in mind when using Session State:

- Session State exists for as long as the tab is open and connected to the Streamlit server. As soon as you close the tab, everything stored in Session State is lost.
- Session State is not persisted. If the Streamlit server crashes, then everything stored in Session State gets wiped

app_session.py — pinned source excerpt
Evidence role: Historical linked source; a reported observation or proposed explanation, not an independently verified fix.

```python
    def shutdown(self) -> None:
        """Shut down the AppSession.

        It's an error to use a AppSession after it's been shut down.

        """
        if self._state != AppSessionState.SHUTDOWN_REQUESTED:
            LOGGER.debug("Shutting down (id=%s)", self.id)
            # Clear any unused session files in upload file manager and media
            # file manager
            self._uploaded_file_mgr.remove_session_files(self.id)

            if runtime.exists():
                runtime.get_instance().media_file_mgr.clear_session_refs(self.id)
                runtime.get_instance().media_file_mgr.remove_orphaned_files()

            # Shut down the ScriptRunner, if one is active.
            # self._state must not be set to SHUTDOWN_REQUESTED until
            # after this is called.
            if self._scriptrunner is not None:
                self._scriptrunner.request_stop()

            self._state = AppSessionState.SHUTDOWN_REQUESTED

            # Disconnect all file watchers if we haven't already, although we will have
            # generally already done so by the time we get here.
            self._disconnect_file_watchers()
```

DEV-16388 — Deleting a widget's session_state key leaves the frontend showing the stale value (backend/frontend divergence for one rerun)

Expected escalate · actual escalate · minor_revision

Correctly retains the one-rerun backend/frontend divergence as an investigation rather than answering with a reset workaround.

Useful part: Recognizes that deletion already occurs through a callback and separates the later rehydration from the unresolved intermediate mismatch.

  • Keep the divergence explicitly user-reported, not independently reproduced. General documentation supports investigation but does not establish the internal cause or precise timing.
  • The bounded callback-assignment reset option could be provided as interim guidance, while preserving the unresolved product concern; its omission does not justify pretending the mismatch is solved.

Actual fresh user reply

Maintainer review is needed: Deleting a keyed widget’s session_state entry inside an on_click callback produces a transient backend/frontend divergence: the backend reports the default value on that rerun while the frontend still shows the previous value, then the next rerun re-adopts the stale frontend value. The shown app already uses supported callbacks, and the observed sequence conflicts with the documented behavior for deleted widget keys, so this cannot be attributed to an obvious app-code ordering mistake; it needs maintainer/product investigation. [R0][R3][R4][R5][R7][R13][S1][S2]
Saved original policy-v3 reply for comparison
Your report matches Streamlit’s documented behavior: when a keyed widget’s Session State entry is deleted, Streamlit recreates it from the widget’s current frontend value, and deleting the key does not revert the widget to its default [R3][R4][R5][S1]. That is why you see one rerun with backend/frontend divergence and then the stale value gets re-adopted on the next rerun [R4][R5][R13].

For this example, the correction is to keep the reset in the callback, but replace `del st.session_state['foo']` with an explicit assignment such as `st.session_state['foo'] = 'default'` (or whatever reset value you want). Streamlit’s button docs show callbacks are the supported place to update another widget’s state [R7][S2].

S1

### Calling a widget command when the widget already exists

When rerunning a script without changing a widget's identity:

1. Streamlit will connect to the existing frontend and backend parts.
2. If the widget has a key that was deleted from `st.session_state`, then Streamlit will recreate the key using the current frontend value. This is because deleting a key from Session State will not revert the widget to a default value.
3. The widget command will return the current value of the widget.

S2

### Buttons to modify or reset other widgets

When a button is used to modify or reset another widget, it is the same as the above examples to modify st.session_state. However, an extra consideration exists: you cannot modify a key-value pair in st.session_state if the widget with that key has already been rendered on the page for the current script run.

S3

#### Option 2: Use a callback

```python
import streamlit as st

st.text_input('Name', key='name')

def set_name(name):
    st.session_state.name = name

st.button('Clear name', on_click=set_name, args=[''])
st.button('Streamlit!', on_click=set_name, args=['Streamlit'])
```

DEV-3903 — Setting widget values using session_state does not work after initialization

Expected request_info · actual answer · needs_revision

Still invents an explicit-default problem in the first reproduction and skips the missing comparison.

Useful part: The second snippet really does combine keyed state and explicit value arguments, which supports a bounded cleanup experiment.

  • R7 has no explicit value argument. The reply instructs removing one from that slider anyway.
  • R9 already assigns values before widget calls. Recommending pre-widget initialization as the resolution fails to explain the reported discrepancy.
  • The documentation warning is not proof of the historical frontend/backend cause or of a verified fix. The isolated comparison belongs in information_gaps, but that array is empty.
  • The renderer preserves the unsupported corrections faithfully; deterministic assembly does not repair semantic omissions.

Actual fresh user reply

In the shown code, each widget is initialized from two sources at once: `st.session_state[...]` and an explicit `value=` argument in the widget call. Streamlit’s session-state docs say this combination is not recommended [S3]. To make the widget reflect the session-state value, initialize `st.session_state` first and declare the widget with the same `key` but without `value=` so the widget reads from session state [S1][S2].

Required edits:
- Keep the session-state initialization before the widget and remove the explicit `value=` default from the slider so the key-bound widget uses the session-state value as its initial state. [R7][S1][S2][S3]
- Use one source of truth for initialization: pre-populate `st.session_state['id_input']` and `st.session_state['my_slider']`, then declare the widgets with those keys only and no `value=` overrides. [R9][S1][S2][S3]
Saved original policy-v3 reply for comparison
The sample does contain a code-level cleanup: for widgets with `key=`, avoid mixing direct `st.session_state.<key>` assignment with explicit `value=` defaults, because the docs say that combination is not recommended and can warn on first run [S2][S3]. The docs also show the standard first-run initialization pattern [S1]. However, the reported symptom is specifically that a pre-widget reassignment in Streamlit 1.0.0 still does not visibly update the widget, and the supplied evidence does not establish whether that behavior is expected for that release or a documentation/behavior gap [R7][R9][R13]. Please route this for maintainer review of widget/session_state synchronization in that version.

S1

### Initialize values in Session State

The Session State API follows a field-based API, which is very similar to Python dictionaries:

```python
# Initialization
if 'key' not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state['key'] = 'value'

# Session State also supports attribute based syntax
if 'key' not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.key = 'value'
```

S2

### Session State and Widget State association

Every widget with a key is automatically added to Session State:

```python
st.text_input("Your name", key="name")

# This exists now:
st.session_state.name
```

S3

- Setting the widget state via the Session State API and using the `value` parameter in the widget declaration is not recommended, and will throw a warning on the first run. For example:

  ```python
  st.session_state.my_slider = 7

  slider = st.slider(
      label='Choose a Value', min_value=1,
      max_value=10, value=5, key='my_slider')
  ```

S4

### Buttons to modify st.session_state

If you modify st.session_state inside of a button, you must consider where that button is within the script.

#### A slight problem

In this example, we access st.session_state.name both before and after the buttons which modify it. When a button ("Jane" or "John") is clicked, the script reruns. The info displayed before the buttons lags behind the info written after the button. The data in st.session_state before the button is not updated. When the script executes the button function, that is when the conditional code to update st.session_state creates the change. Thus, this change is reflected after the button.

```python
import streamlit as st
import pandas as pd

if 'name' not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state['name'] = 'John Doe'

st.header(st.session_state['name'])

if st.button('Jane'):
    st.session_state['name'] = 'Jane Doe'

if st.button('John'):
    st.session_state['name'] = 'John Doe'

st.header(st.session_state['name'])
```

#### Logic used in a callback

Callbacks are a clean way to modify st.session_state. Callbacks are executed as a prefix to the script rerunning, so the position of the button relative to accessing data is not important.

```python
import streamlit as st
import pandas as pd

if 'name' not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state['name'] = 'John Doe'

def change_name(name):
    st.session_state['name'] = name

st.header(st.session_state['name'])

st.button('Jane', on_click=change_name, args=['Jane Doe'])
st.button('John', on_click=change_name, args=['John Doe'])

st.header(st.session_state['name'])
```

DEV-4325 — Utilizing Multiselect as a callback for a Session State only lets user choose 1 option

Expected answer · actual answer · needs_revision

Retains answer routing, but the fresh repeat drops the persistent outer-stage correction.

Useful part: The reply includes form batching, fresh keyed callback reads and a general correction of the state-name mismatch, and all identified edits reach the user reply.

  • The outer Start Labeling button gate remains a critical blocker. Neither the answer nor its findings instructs persisting that stage in this fresh sample, unlike the earlier identical-request three-case output.
  • The singular/plural mismatch is identified in the raw finding, but the final correction is generic instead of naming current_image/current_images.
  • Storage/counter initialization and next-item advancement remain high-level. Three of four finding slots cover overlapping form/value wiring; an essential enclosing-state edit is lost.
  • A schema-valid answer with all generated edits preserved can still be incomplete. No corrected app was executed.

Actual fresh user reply

`st.multiselect` is outside a form in the shown code, so Streamlit reruns the script on every selection; that is why the user cannot finish selecting multiple options before the app reacts [S1][S2]. To defer processing until the user is done, place the multiselect and submit control inside `st.form(...)` and handle the values from `st.form_submit_button`; inside a form, only the submit button can have a callback [S2][S4]. If the callback needs the selected labels, give the multiselect a key and read the updated value from `st.session_state` inside the callback rather than passing the widget value directly [S3][S8].

Required edits:
- Wrap the multiselect and submit control in `st.form(...)` so selections are buffered until the user submits the form. [R2][S1][S2][S4]
- Use `st.form_submit_button` as the only callback-capable control inside the form, and have the callback read the multiselect value from `st.session_state` via a widget key. [R6][S2][S3][S4][S8]
- Pass the actual selected value path from the keyed widget state, or read the keyed multiselect value inside `annotate()` before updating `st.session_state.annotations`. [R6][S3][S8]
- Use one consistent session-state key name throughout the stage progression and rendering loop so the advanced item is the same object that later code reads. [R6][S8]
Saved original policy-v3 reply for comparison
Use a form-based submit flow and make the labeling UI persist across reruns. The current `st.button('Start Labeling')` gate is ephemeral, so the UI disappears on the next rerun [S5][S7]. Initialize a persistent `st.session_state` flag/stage, set it from the Start Labeling button, and render the annotation widgets whenever that flag is true [S6][S8]. Put the multiselect and the Submit button inside `st.form(...)`; that prevents reruns on each selection change and ensures the callback only happens when the form is submitted [S1][S2][S4]. Give the multiselect a `key` and read the submitted selection from `st.session_state.<key>` in the submit handler instead of passing an undefined `labels` argument [S3][S8]. Finally, fix the state-name mismatch (`current_image` vs `current_images`) so the next item is written and read from the same key; otherwise progression will not show the new item.

S1

## User interaction

If a widget is not in a form, that widget will trigger a script rerun whenever a user changes its value. For widgets with keyed input (`st.number_input`, `st.text_input`, `st.text_area`), a new value triggers a rerun when the user clicks or tabs out of the widget. A user can also submit a change by pressing `Enter` while their cursor is active in the widget.

On the other hand if a widget is inside of a form, the script will not rerun when a user clicks or tabs out of that widget. For widgets inside a form, the script will rerun when the form is submitted and all widgets within the form will send their updated values to the Python backend.

A user can submit a form using **Enter** on their keyboard if their cursor active in a widget that accepts keyed input. Within `st.number_input` and `st.text_input` a user presses **Enter** to submit the form. Within `st.text_area` a user presses **Ctrl+Enter**/**⌘+Enter** to submit the form.

S2

## Processing form submissions

The purpose of a form is to override the default behavior of Streamlit which reruns a script as soon as the user makes a change. For widgets outside of a form, the logical flow is:

1. The user changes a widget's value on the frontend.
2. The widget's value in `st.session_state` and in the Python backend (server) is updated.
3. The script rerun begins.
4. If the widget has a callback, it is executed as a prefix to the page rerun.
5. When the updated widget's function is executed during the rerun, it outputs the new value.

For widgets inside a form, any changes made by a user (step 1) do not get passed to the Python backend (step 2) until the form is submitted. Furthermore, the only widget inside a form that can have a callback function is the `st.form_submit_button`. If you need to execute a process using newly submitted values, you have three major patterns for doing so.

S3

### Use a callback with session state

You can use a callback to execute a process as a prefix to the script rerunning.

When processing newly updated values within a callback, do not pass those values to the callback directly through the `args` or `kwargs` parameters. You need to assign a key to any widget whose value you use within the callback. If you look up the value of that widget from `st.session_state` within the body of the callback, you will be able to access the newly submitted value. See the example below.

```python
import streamlit as st

if 'sum' not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.sum = ''

def sum():
    result = st.session_state.a + st.session_state.b
    st.session_state.sum = result

col1,col2 = st.columns(2)
col1.title('Sum:')
if isinstance(st.session_state.sum, float):
    col2.title(f'{st.session_state.sum:.2f}')

with st.form('addition'):
    st.number_input('a', key = 'a')
    st.number_input('b', key = 'b')
    st.form_submit_button('add', on_click=sum)
```

S4

## Limitations

- Every form must contain a `st.form_submit_button`.
- `st.button` and `st.download_button` cannot be added to a form.
- `st.form` cannot be embedded inside another `st.form`.
- Callback functions can only be assigned to `st.form_submit_button` within a form; no other widgets in a form can have a callback.
- Interdependent widgets within a form are unlikely to be particularly useful. If you pass `widget1`'s value into `widget2` when they are both inside a form, then `widget2` will only update when the form is submitted.

S5

## Summary

Buttons created with st.button do not retain state. They return True on the script rerun resulting from their click and immediately return to False on the next script rerun. If a displayed element is nested inside if st.button('Click me'):, the element will be visible when the button is clicked and disappear as soon as the user takes their next action. This is because the script reruns and the button return value becomes False.

In this guide, we will illustrate the use of buttons and explain common misconceptions. Read on to see a variety of examples that expand on st.button using st.session_state. Anti-patterns are included at the end. Go ahead and pull up your favorite code editor so you can streamlit run the examples as you read. Check out Streamlit's Basic concepts if you haven't run your own Streamlit scripts yet.

S6

### Buttons to continue or control stages of a process

Another alternative to nesting content inside a button is to use a value in st.session_state that designates the "step" or "stage" of a process. In this example, we have four stages in our script:

Before the user begins.

User enters their name.

User chooses a color.

User gets a thank-you message.

A button at the beginning advances the stage from 0 to 1. A button at the end resets the stage from 3 to 0. The other widgets used in stage 1 and 2 have callbacks to set the stage. If you have a process with dependant steps and want to keep previous stages visible, such a callback forces a user to retrace subsequent stages if they change an earlier widget.

```python
import streamlit as st

if 'stage' not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.stage = 0

def set_state(i):
    st.session_state.stage = i

if st.session_state.stage == 0:
    st.button('Begin', on_click=set_state, args=[1])

if st.session_state.stage >= 1:
    name = st.text_input('Name', on_change=set_state, args=[2])

if st.session_state.stage >= 2:
    st.write(f'Hello {name}!')
    color = st.selectbox(
        'Pick a Color',
        [None, 'red', 'orange', 'green', 'blue', 'violet'],
        on_change=set_state, args=[3]
    )
    if color is None:
        set_state(2)

if st.session_state.stage >= 3:
    st.write(f':{color}[Thank you!]')
    st.button('Start Over', on_click=set_state, args=[0])
```

S7

### Other widgets nested inside buttons

```python
import streamlit as st

if st.button('Sign up'):
    name = st.text_input('Name')

    if name:
        # This will never be executed.
        st.success(f'Welcome {name}')
```

S8

### Use Callbacks to update Session State

A callback is a python function which gets called when an input widget changes.

**Order of execution**: When updating Session state in response to **events**, a callback function gets executed first, and then the app is executed from top to bottom.

Callbacks can be used with widgets using the parameters `on_change` (or `on_click`), `args`, and `kwargs`:

**Parameters**

Actual request · Raw response · Rendered record · Reference map

DEV-7305 — on_change not able to access text_area text on initalization and later on uses old text_area value

Expected answer · actual answer · usable_by_inspection

Supported correction of immediate function invocation, widget key binding and the manual same-key assignment.

Useful part: Uses the callable reference instead of update(), reads fresh keyed state in the callback and removes the problematic outer return-value write.

  • The reported key-only attempt was not sufficient; function registration and keyed reading must be applied together. No historical app execution or initial-display verification was performed.

Actual fresh user reply

The shown code is registering the callback incorrectly and is not using widget-state association. `on_change=update()` executes `update` immediately during widget creation, so no callback is registered for later edits; and because the widget has no `key`, `st.session_state['text_area']` is not automatically linked to the widget’s live value [S1][S2][S3][S5]. Use `key='text_area'`, pass the callable itself (`on_change=update`), and read `st.session_state.text_area` inside `update` [S1][S2][S3][S4][S5].

Required edits:
- Pass the callback object without parentheses (`on_change=update`) so Streamlit can run it on the widget change event before the app reruns. [R5][S2][S5]
- Give the widget `key='text_area'` and read `st.session_state.text_area` in the callback; remove the manual `st.session_state['text_area'] = ...` assignment. [R5][S1][S3][S4][S5]
Saved original policy-v3 reply for comparison
The shown code supports a correction, not a framework-side workaround: register the callback correctly, use the widget key for state, and stop assigning the widget return value into `st.session_state` yourself. A minimal integrated edit is:

```python
import streamlit as st

def update():
    st.write(st.session_state.text_area)

st.text_area(
    "example test",
    value="hello from the textbox",
    key="text_area",
    on_change=update,
)
```

Key points: `on_change=update` must pass the function itself, not `update()`; the keyed text area is then available as `st.session_state.text_area`; and if you want text shown before any user interaction, render that separately because callbacks only run after a widget event and before the rerun [S2][S4].

### Session State and Widget State association

### Use Callbacks to update Session State

A callback is a python function which gets called when an input widget changes.

**Order of execution**: When updating Session state in response to **events**, a callback function gets executed first, and then the app is executed from top to bottom.

Callbacks can be used with widgets using the parameters `on_change` (or `on_click`), `args`, and `kwargs`:

**Parameters**

- **on_change** or **on_click** - The function name to be used as a callback
- **args** (_tuple_) - List of arguments to be passed to the callback function
- **kwargs** (_dict_) - Named arguments to be passed to the callback function

S3

A key lets you read or update the widget's value via
st.session_state[key]. For more details, see [Widget
behavior](https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/concepts/architecture/widget-behavior).

S4

- "rerun" (default): Streamlit will rerun the app when the
user commits a new value (blurring the field, or pressing
Ctrl+Enter / Cmd+Enter).

S5

- A callable: Streamlit will rerun the app and execute the
callable as a callback function before the rest of the app.

The current docs state that `on_click` is an optional callback invoked when the button is clicked, and that `st.form_submit_button` is the way a form is submitted [S1][S2]. Because the report is on Streamlit 0.84.1 [R11] and the supplied evidence does not establish whether this is a version-specific bug, a documentation mismatch, or a later behavior change, I can’t support a reliable app-side correction from the evidence here. Please hand this to maintainer review for historical behavior/compatibility verification of `form_submit_button` callbacks in 0.84.1.

S1

st.form_submit_button

## st.form_submit_button

Display a form submit button.

When this button is clicked, all widget values inside the form will be
sent from the user's browser to your Streamlit server in a batch.

Every form must have at least one st.form_submit_button. It is the
only way to submit a form: without it, the widget values inside the
form are never sent to your app, so the form is non-functional. An
st.form_submit_button cannot exist outside of a form.

For more information about forms, check out our docs.

S2

### Forms and Callbacks

Widgets inside a form can have their values be accessed and set via the Session State API. `st.form_submit_button` can have a callback associated with it. The callback gets executed upon clicking on the submit button. For example:

```python
def form_callback():
    st.write(st.session_state.my_slider)
    st.write(st.session_state.my_checkbox)

with st.form(key='my_form'):
    slider_input = st.slider('My slider', 0, 10, 5, key='my_slider')
    checkbox_input = st.checkbox('Yes or No', key='my_checkbox')
    submit_button = st.form_submit_button(label='Submit', on_click=form_callback)
```

DEV-3842 — Session State not working as expected in Streamlit 0.89.0

Expected answer · actual answer · usable_by_inspection

Correctly fixes unconditional count reset and preserves the state-driven form gate.

Useful part: Explicit guarded initialization and the retained update-click path explain the visible code error without asking irrelevant questions.

  • The edit list is supported by the supplied code and references but was not run as a historical Streamlit application.

Actual fresh user reply

The disappearing form is explained by the code resetting `st.session_state['count'] = 0` on every rerun. When `Display Count` is clicked, Streamlit reruns the script, that assignment clears the flag before `if st.session_state['count'] == 1:` is evaluated, so the form is no longer rendered. Initialize `count` only once with a `'count' not in st.session_state` check, then update it when `Update Count` is clicked. Session state is persistent across reruns, while button clicks are transient [S1][S2][S3][S4].

Required edits:
- Guard initialization: `if 'count' not in st.session_state: st.session_state['count'] = 0`, then keep the `Update Count` assignment that sets it to 1 when clicked. [R5][S1][S2][S3]
- Render the form from the persistent session-state flag rather than from a value that is reinitialized each run; the form should stay inside the `count == 1` branch only after `count` is preserved across reruns. [R9][S1][S3][S4]
Saved original policy-v3 reply for comparison
The form disappears because `count` is being reset to `0` on every rerun, so the `if st.session_state["count"] == 1:` branch becomes false right after the submit rerun [R2][R9]. Streamlit’s Session State docs recommend initializing keys only once and then updating them later [S1][S2], and button-driven visibility needs persistent state because button values do not stay true across reruns [S3][S4].

Apply these changes together:

1. Initialize `count` only if it does not already exist.
2. Leave the `Update Count` action to set the stored value to `1`.
3. Keep the form inside the conditional that reads the persistent state.

Partial example:

```python
import streamlit as st

if "count" not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state["count"] = 0

if st.button("Update Count"):
    st.session_state["count"] = 1

if st.session_state["count"] == 1:
    with st.form("form"):
        submitted = st.form_submit_button("Display Count")
        if submitted:
            st.write(st.session_state["count"])
```

With that change, the form will stay visible after the submit rerun because the state gate no longer gets cleared first [S1][S2][S3].

S1

### Initialize values in Session State

The Session State API follows a field-based API, which is very similar to Python dictionaries:

```python
# Initialization
if 'key' not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state['key'] = 'value'

# Session State also supports attribute based syntax
if 'key' not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.key = 'value'
```

S2

Update an item in Session State by assigning it a value:

```python
st.session_state.key = 'value2'     # Attribute API
st.session_state['key'] = 'value2'  # Dictionary like API
```

S3

## Summary

Buttons created with st.button do not retain state. They return True on the script rerun resulting from their click and immediately return to False on the next script rerun. If a displayed element is nested inside if st.button('Click me'):, the element will be visible when the button is clicked and disappear as soon as the user takes their next action. This is because the script reruns and the button return value becomes False.

In this guide, we will illustrate the use of buttons and explain common misconceptions. Read on to see a variety of examples that expand on st.button using st.session_state. Anti-patterns are included at the end. Go ahead and pull up your favorite code editor so you can streamlit run the examples as you read. Check out Streamlit's Basic concepts if you haven't run your own Streamlit scripts yet.

S4

### Stateful button

If you want a clicked button to continue to be True, create a value in st.session_state and use the button to set that value to True in a callback.

```python
import streamlit as st

if 'clicked' not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.clicked = False

def click_button():
    st.session_state.clicked = True

st.button('Click me', on_click=click_button)

if st.session_state.clicked:
    # The message and nested widget will remain on the page
    st.write('Button clicked!')
    st.slider('Select a value')
```

DEV-4082 — Form updates session state only after every second submission

Expected answer · actual answer · needs_revision

Useful submit-time copying is mixed with an overbroad restriction and an incomplete stable-widget correction.

Useful part: Separates collecting form values from writing application data on a successful submission.

  • The reply says not to rely on the widget return variable, while its own first edit permits binding a local variable. Post-submit return-value processing is supported; callback freshness guidance must not be generalized to all form processing.
  • The original widget receives value=data, which changes as application data changes. The reply does not explicitly stabilize/remove that changing default or preserve the intended initial value, leaving the historical alternating behavior insufficiently addressed.
  • Calling this the established cause/fix of the historical behavior overstates the supplied evidence. No corrected form was executed.

Actual fresh user reply

The shown code mixes two different state paths: the widget is keyed as `name`, but the app copies the widget return into `st.session_state['data']` inside the form. In forms, widget edits are buffered until submit, and when you need the newly submitted value you should read the widget by its key from `st.session_state`, not rely on the variable assigned to the widget call [S1][S2][S3]. A supported fix is to keep the text input keyed as `name`, then after `st.form_submit_button(...)` copy `st.session_state.name` into `st.session_state['data']` (or use one session-state key consistently).

Required edits:
- Use the keyed widget value as the source of truth: bind the input to a local variable or read `st.session_state.name`, then copy that value into `st.session_state['data']` after the form is submitted, instead of treating the text_input return as the persistent session-state source. [R5][S1][S2][S3]
- Capture `submit = st.form_submit_button('Submit')`, keep the input collection inside the form, and perform the `data` update only after the form block when `submit` is true so the newly submitted value is written once per submission. [R6][S1][S2]
Saved original policy-v3 reply for comparison
Your snippet is updating `st.session_state['data']` from the `st.text_input(...)` return value inside the form [R5], but Streamlit forms only send edited values to the backend on submit [S1]. The supported pattern is to give the widget a key and then read that keyed value from `st.session_state` when the form is submitted [S2][S3].

A working edit is:

```python
import streamlit as st

if "data" not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.data = "empty"

with st.form("myform"):
    st.text_input("Enter name", key="name")
    submitted = st.form_submit_button("Submit")

if submitted:
    st.session_state.data = st.session_state.name
    st.write("Submitted!")

st.write(st.session_state.data)
```

If you want the text box to start from `data`, initialize `st.session_state.name` once before creating the form, but do not keep copying `data` into the widget on every rerun. The important change is to remove the inline assignment from the widget call and perform the `data` copy only at submit time [S1][S2][S3].

S1

## Processing form submissions

The purpose of a form is to override the default behavior of Streamlit which reruns a script as soon as the user makes a change. For widgets outside of a form, the logical flow is:

1. The user changes a widget's value on the frontend.
2. The widget's value in `st.session_state` and in the Python backend (server) is updated.
3. The script rerun begins.
4. If the widget has a callback, it is executed as a prefix to the page rerun.
5. When the updated widget's function is executed during the rerun, it outputs the new value.

For widgets inside a form, any changes made by a user (step 1) do not get passed to the Python backend (step 2) until the form is submitted. Furthermore, the only widget inside a form that can have a callback function is the `st.form_submit_button`. If you need to execute a process using newly submitted values, you have three major patterns for doing so.

### Execute the process after the form

If you need to execute a one-time process as a result of a form submission, you can condition that process on the `st.form_submit_button` and execute it after the form. If you need results from your process to display above the form, you can use containers to control where the form displays relative to your output.

```python
import streamlit as st

col1,col2 = st.columns([1,2])
col1.title('Sum:')

with st.form('addition'):
    a = st.number_input('a')
    b = st.number_input('b')
    submit = st.form_submit_button('add')

if submit:
    col2.title(f'{a+b:.2f}')
```

S2

### Use a callback with session state

You can use a callback to execute a process as a prefix to the script rerunning.

When processing newly updated values within a callback, do not pass those values to the callback directly through the `args` or `kwargs` parameters. You need to assign a key to any widget whose value you use within the callback. If you look up the value of that widget from `st.session_state` within the body of the callback, you will be able to access the newly submitted value. See the example below.

```python
import streamlit as st

if 'sum' not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.sum = ''

def sum():
    result = st.session_state.a + st.session_state.b
    st.session_state.sum = result

col1,col2 = st.columns(2)
col1.title('Sum:')
if isinstance(st.session_state.sum, float):
    col2.title(f'{st.session_state.sum:.2f}')

with st.form('addition'):
    st.number_input('a', key = 'a')
    st.number_input('b', key = 'b')
    st.form_submit_button('add', on_click=sum)
```

S3

## Solution

When using session state to update widgets or values in your script, you need to use the unique key you assigned to the widget, **not** the variable that you assigned your widget to.

S4

**Key-based widget identity (v1.55.0)**

As of v1.55.0, all widgets support key-based identity. When a `key` is provided, the key is the primary determinant of the widget's identity, and changing other parameters (like `label`, `options`, or `default`) won't reset the widget. Some parameters that constrain valid values still affect identity for specific widgets, even when a key is provided. For example, changing `min_value` or `max_value` for `st.slider` will reset the widget because the current value could be invalidated. These exceptions are noted in each widget's `key` parameter description.

Key-based identity was progressively introduced from v1.50.0 through v1.55.0. If you're using an older version, check the [release notes](/develop/quick-reference/release-notes) to see which widgets support key-based identity in your version.

S5

### Changing a widget's identity will reset it

If any of the parameters that determine a widget's identity change, Streamlit will see it as a new widget and it will reset. Providing a key protects the widget from resets when most parameters change. The use of default values is particularly important in this case. If you use a key and change a widget's default value, there will be no change to the widget's state. If you don't use a key, changing a widget's default value will reset the widget to that default value.

S1

# Working with widgets in multipage apps

When you create a widget in a Streamlit app, Streamlit generates a widget ID and uses it to make your widget stateful. As your app reruns with user interaction, Streamlit keeps track of the widget's value by associating its value to its ID. In particular, a widget's ID depends on the page where it's created. If you define an identical widget on two different pages, then the widget will reset to its default value when you switch pages.

This guide explains three strategies to deal with the behavior if you'd like to have a widget remain stateful across all pages. If don't want a widget to appear on all pages, but you do want it to remain stateful when you navigate away from its page (and then back), Options 2 and 3 can be used. For detailed information about these strategies, see [Understanding widget behavior](/develop/concepts/architecture/widget-behavior).

S2

## Option 2: Save your widget values into a dummy key in Session State

If you want to navigate away from a widget and return to it while keeping its value, or if you want to use the same widget on multiple pages, use a separate key in `st.session_state` to save the value independently from the widget. In this example, a temporary key is used with a widget. The temporary key uses an underscore prefix. Hence, `"_my_key"` is used as the widget key, but the data is copied to `"my_key"` to preserve it between pages.

```python
import streamlit as st

def store_value():
    # Copy the value to the permanent key
    st.session_state["my_key"] = st.session_state["_my_key"]

# Copy the saved value to the temporary key
st.session_state["_my_key"] = st.session_state["my_key"]
st.number_input("Number of filters", key="_my_key", on_change=store_value)
```

S3

## Option 3: Interrupt the widget clean-up process

When Streamlit gets to the end of an app run, it will delete the data for any widgets that were not rendered. This includes data for any widget not associated to the current page. However, if you re-save a key-value pair in an app run, Streamlit will not associate the key-value pair to any widget until you execute a widget command again with that key.

As a result, if you have the following code at the top of every page, any widget with the key `"my_key"` will retain its value wherever it's rendered (or not). Alternatively, if you are using `st.navigation` and `st.Page`, you can include this once in your entrypoint file before executing your page.

```python
if "my_key" in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.my_key = st.session_state.my_key
```

S4

## Solution

When using session state to update widgets or values in your script, you need to use the unique key you assigned to the widget, **not** the variable that you assigned your widget to.

DEV-4989 — widget state not synced between multiple pages

Expected answer · actual answer · minor_revision

Useful page-widget/durable-state distinction with incomplete migration and existing-workaround qualification.

Useful part: Uses the pre-1.46 identity note for the reported 1.11.0 setup and describes a consistent permanent/temp-key mirror.

  • The optional st.Page/st.navigation approach requires both an architecture change and a compatible-version upgrade; the latter is not explicit.
  • The report already tried re-saving state, which the sources also document. Do not imply a separate permanent key is the only possible bridge or dismiss the tested self-assignment effect as navigation alone.
  • The advice was not executed on the original app and the repeated edit list could be more concise.

Actual fresh user reply

This is expected for an app built with the `pages/` directory: each page creates its own widget identity, so the two `st.text_input(..., key='shared_input')` calls do not share widget state across pages even though `st.session_state` itself is shared [R6][R9][R11][S1][S7]. In Streamlit 1.11.0, a widget value coming from another page is ignored for the new page’s widget identity [S6]. To keep the value across pages, use the documented session-state mirror pattern: bind the widget to a page-local temporary key and copy its value into a separate permanent key, or move the widget into a common entrypoint only if you switch to `st.navigation`/`st.Page` [S2][S3][S4].

Required edits:
- Do not rely on identical widget keys across pages in a `pages/`-directory app; give each page its own widget key and mirror the value into a separate durable `st.session_state` key, or centralize the widget in the entrypoint only if the app is converted to `st.navigation`/`st.Page`. [R6][S1][S2][S3][S6][S7]
- Seed the page widget from a persistent session-state value on each page run, then copy the widget value back to that persistent key on change; do not expect page navigation alone to carry widget state across identities. [R9][S3][S4][S6][S7]
- Treat this as widget-identity behavior rather than a broken session-state share; use the documented dummy-key/session-state mirror pattern so the durable value and the rendered widget are kept in sync explicitly. [R13][S1][S3][S4][S7]
- Keep the navigation check only as page-routing logic; the actual state bridge still needs a separate persistent key plus a widget-local key, with the widget constructed from the persistent value and its changes copied back through the callback or mirror step. [R21][S3][S4][S6]
Saved original policy-v3 reply for comparison
This behavior is expected for the reported setup and version: in multipage apps, a widget’s ID depends on the page, so an identical widget on another page resets to its default when you navigate [S1]. Streamlit 1.11.0 is also in the pre-1.46.0 behavior where a value coming from another page’s widget instance is ignored because it has a different identity [S6]. The pages still share `st.session_state` [S7], so the fix is to persist the value separately and hydrate the widget from that value before the widget is created on each page [S3].

Partial example (for the `pages/` directory):
```py
import streamlit as st

if "shared_input" in st.session_state:
    st.session_state["_shared_input"] = st.session_state["shared_input"]

def store_value():
    st.session_state["shared_input"] = st.session_state["_shared_input"]

st.text_input("inp", key="_shared_input", on_change=store_value)
```
Integration requirements: run the restore step on every page before the widget command; keep `shared_input` as the permanent value and `_shared_input` as the widget key; if you want the widget itself to live across pages, move it into an entrypoint using `st.Page`/`st.navigation` instead of the `pages/` directory [S2].

S1

# Working with widgets in multipage apps

When you create a widget in a Streamlit app, Streamlit generates a widget ID and uses it to make your widget stateful. As your app reruns with user interaction, Streamlit keeps track of the widget's value by associating its value to its ID. In particular, a widget's ID depends on the page where it's created. If you define an identical widget on two different pages, then the widget will reset to its default value when you switch pages.

This guide explains three strategies to deal with the behavior if you'd like to have a widget remain stateful across all pages. If don't want a widget to appear on all pages, but you do want it to remain stateful when you navigate away from its page (and then back), Options 2 and 3 can be used. For detailed information about these strategies, see [Understanding widget behavior](/develop/concepts/architecture/widget-behavior).

S2

## Option 1 (preferred): Execute your widget command in your entrypoint file

When you define your multipage app with `st.Page` and `st.navigation`, your entrypoint file becomes a frame of common elements around your pages. When you execute a widget command in your entrypoint file, Streamlit associates the widget to your entrypoint file instead of a particular page. Since your entrypoint file is executed in every app rerun, any widget in your entrypoint file will remain stateful as your users switch between pages.

This method does not work if you define your app with the `pages/` directory.

S3

## Option 2: Save your widget values into a dummy key in Session State

If you want to navigate away from a widget and return to it while keeping its value, or if you want to use the same widget on multiple pages, use a separate key in `st.session_state` to save the value independently from the widget. In this example, a temporary key is used with a widget. The temporary key uses an underscore prefix. Hence, `"_my_key"` is used as the widget key, but the data is copied to `"my_key"` to preserve it between pages.

```python
import streamlit as st

def store_value():
    # Copy the value to the permanent key
    st.session_state["my_key"] = st.session_state["_my_key"]

# Copy the saved value to the temporary key
st.session_state["_my_key"] = st.session_state["my_key"]
st.number_input("Number of filters", key="_my_key", on_change=store_value)
```

S4

## Option 3: Interrupt the widget clean-up process

When Streamlit gets to the end of an app run, it will delete the data for any widgets that were not rendered. This includes data for any widget not associated to the current page. However, if you re-save a key-value pair in an app run, Streamlit will not associate the key-value pair to any widget until you execute a widget command again with that key.

As a result, if you have the following code at the top of every page, any widget with the key `"my_key"` will retain its value wherever it's rendered (or not). Alternatively, if you are using `st.navigation` and `st.Page`, you can include this once in your entrypoint file before executing your page.

```python
if "my_key" in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.my_key = st.session_state.my_key
```

S6

### Calling a widget command when the widget doesn't already exist

If your script rerun calls a widget command with a changed identity or calls a widget command that wasn't used on the last script run:

1. Streamlit will build the frontend and backend parts of the widget, using its default value.
2. If the widget has been assigned a key, Streamlit will check if that key already exists in Session State.
   a. If the key exists and **isn't** associated to a widget with a different identity, Streamlit will assign that key's value to the widget.
   b. If the key exists and is associated to a widget with a different identity, Streamlit will overwrite the key-value pair with the default value. This is why writing to Session State before the widget command is important when [retaining statefulness across identity changes](#retain-statefulness-when-changing-a-widgets-identity).
   c. If the key doesn't exist, Streamlit will create a new key-value pair with the default value.
3. If there are args or kwargs for a callback function, they are evaluated and saved in memory.
4. The widget value is then returned by the function.

For step 2, prior to v1.46.0, Streamlit would ignore the value in Session State if it came from an instance of the widget on another page. This is because a widget on another page necessarily has a different identity. As of v1.46.0, Streamlit deletes such values at the beginning of a script run on a new page.

S7

- Pages share the same [st.session_state](/develop/concepts/architecture/session-state):

  ```python
  # page1.py

  if "shared" not in st.session_state:
  ```
